capabilities.target: Postgres database via execute_sql, service role (bypasses RLS); includes tickets, support_messages, and integration_tokens tables
insert into support_messages, rendered back to the customer who filed the ticket

inputs.source: Developer natural-language request in the IDE chat ("Show me the latest open support tickets.")
Customer-submitted ticket message via the public support widget; stored in the database and later read by the agent

controls.name: IDE per-tool-call approval prompt (shows SQL)
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced in the IDE client outside the model and shows the raw SQL text, so it does not decay with model capability. Its practical effectiveness instead depends on approval volume per session: the runtime notes state developers approve many calls in a session, which is the documented approval-fatigue failure mode (SAFE-T1403) behind this exact public incident.

controls.name: Least-privilege, RLS-enforcing database role for execute_sql
controls.decay_rationale: A credential scoped to only the tables needed for ticket triage, with RLS enforced and no grant on integration_tokens or other secret tables, would make the sensitive read unreachable regardless of model or developer behavior.

controls.name: Pinned/hashed Supabase MCP server version
controls.decay_rationale: Pinning the server to an audited version or content hash, instead of '@latest', prevents silent tool redefinition from an upstream compromise or routine update (rug pull).

controls.name: Cross-capability taint/content check before customer-visible writes
controls.decay_rationale: A monitor outside the model that blocks writes to customer-visible tables whose content was derived from a sensitive-table read in the same session. Enforced structurally, but an obfuscated or re-encoded payload could evade pattern-based inspection.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1) plus confused deputy (TC4): injected ticket content exfiltrates integration tokens via service-role execute_sql and a customer-visible reply

attack_path.note: An attacker-controlled customer submits a ticket via the public support widget containing an embedded instruction, e.g. to look up and relay integration token values.

The developer's benign request ('show me the latest open support tickets') causes the agent to call execute_sql under the service role, which bypasses RLS. The ticket content enters the agent's context, and following the embedded instruction the agent also queries the integration_tokens table, which the service role can read.
The agent inserts a reply into support_messages containing the retrieved token values. That table is rendered back to the customer who filed the ticket, completing egress to the attacker.

forecast.watch_signal: The IDE's approval setting is changed to auto-approve or batch-approve, the per-call prompt is disabled or made optional, review is reduced to a collapsed-link summary rather than full SQL text, or developers report routinely rubber-stamping approvals during long sessions.

evidence.observation: Server is invoked with --access-token pointing to a long-lived PAT; runtime notes confirm this grants service-role access.
"The database connection uses the service role, which bypasses row level security. A table of integration tokens sits in the same database."
"Customers write ticket messages through the public support widget. Rows in support_messages are shown back to the customer."

"The IDE client asks the developer to approve each tool call and shows the SQL. Developers approve many calls in a session." This is the SAFE-T1403 consent-fatigue pattern and is why likelihood is scored above the rubric's default 'unlikely' for a raw-action gate.

recommendations.action: Replace the service-role credential used by execute_sql with a least-privilege, RLS-enforcing role scoped to only the tables needed for ticket triage; deny access to integration_tokens and other credential/secret tables.
Pin the Supabase MCP server to an audited version or content hash instead of '@latest'; verify provenance before each session.

Add a structural check outside the model that blocks any write to a customer-visible table (support_messages) whose content was derived, in the same session, from a read of a table flagged as sensitive.
Log and alert on execute_sql calls touching integration_tokens or other secret tables, and on sessions where a sensitive read is followed by a write to a customer-visible table.
Spotlight/delimit ticket message content as untrusted data in the agent's context and instruct the model explicitly that ticket text is never an instruction.
Reduce approval fatigue: require a distinct, non-collapsible confirmation step specifically when a call reads a table tagged as sensitive, rather than uniform raw-SQL review across all calls.

findings.title: Unpinned MCP server (ASI04): npx -y @latest plus a command-line PAT grants a standing supply-chain path to arbitrary service-role SQL execution

attack_path.note: Configuration runs 'npx -y @supabase/mcp-server-supabase@latest', re-resolving to whatever package version is published at invocation time; no hash or version pin, and no signature or identity verification is declared.

If the published package or a dependency were compromised (tool redefinition / rug pull), the attacker-controlled server code would execute with the same service-role credential already granted to this tool.
A compromised server could use any bound capability, including the customer-visible reply path, for exfiltration or further abuse.

threat_refs.name: AI Supply Chain Compromise: AI Agent Tool

forecast.watch_signal: The resolved package version actually changes between sessions (no lockfile pin), or a new tool/parameter appears in the server's tools/list response without review.

evidence.observation: '@supabase/mcp-server-supabase@latest' — the version tag is 'latest', not a pinned version or content hash.
'--access-token ${SUPABASE_PAT}' passes a static personal access token as a command-line argument, visible in process listings and shell history, with no declared scope restriction or rotation.

recommendations.action: Pin the MCP server package to a specific version and hash, verify it at startup, and disallow auto-updating '@latest' invocations in developer tooling.
Move the Supabase PAT out of command-line arguments into a secret manager or environment variable with restricted read permissions, and scope and rotate the token.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is critical: an untrusted, customer-authored ticket message can reach a service-role execute_sql capability that bypasses row-level security and a customer-visible reply capability, forming a lethal trifecta (TC1) compounded by a confused-deputy privilege gap (TC4, broad service-role credential). The only present control on that path is a per-call approval prompt that shows raw SQL (structural, independent for model capability), which the rubric credits -2 tiers to a residual of moderate for that specific finding. However, the rollup is held at critical by a second, uncontrolled finding: the MCP server is fetched unpinned ('@latest') with a command-line-exposed PAT, a standing ASI04 supply-chain path for which no control exists at all. The forecast stays critical for both reasons: the approval gate is a documented point of failure under high call volume in this exact family of incidents (SAFE-T1403, evidenced directly by 'developers approve many calls in a session') and would be defeated outright by autonomy_increase or control_removal, while the supply-chain path requires only a routine package update to be exercised. Likelihood for the trifecta finding is scored 'likely' rather than the rubric's raw-action default of 'unlikely' because the artifact's own runtime notes describe the approval-fatigue condition that caused this class of incident to succeed in practice.

limitations: This assessment reflects declared design and configuration (the MCP config and runtime notes) as provided, not observed runtime behavior, logs, or live testing.

No system prompt text was supplied beyond the single developer request; instruction-level issues such as spotlighting of untrusted ticket content could not be directly evaluated and are assumed absent from the design.

The database schema and RLS policies for roles other than the service role were not provided; the assumption that no other mitigating role or view separates integration_tokens from ticket data is inferred from the runtime notes.

Whether the IDE's approval prompt displays complete, untruncated SQL (including inserted literal values) for every call, or truncates long values, was not verified; this affects whether the raw_action classification fully holds in practice.
No information was provided on logging, monitoring, or alerting for execute_sql calls, so detective control coverage is assessed as absent rather than confirmed absent.
